_note: Original top-up questions: every skill reaches at least 25 questions (Below / On / Above). Loaded by scripts/skills/top-up-skills.ts, which adds only what each skill is missing.

questions.stem: A poet wants to describe the ocean. Which line uses the sense of sound?
options: The waves crash and hiss on the sand.

questions.stem: Which pair of words rhymes and could end two lines of a poem?
questions.why: Night and bright end with the same sound.

questions.stem: What is a stanza in a poem?
options: a group of lines together, like a paragraph

questions.stem: Which line would make a good first line for a poem about autumn?
options: Red leaves spin like dancers in the wind.
There are four seasons in a year.
questions.why: It paints a picture with vivid words.

questions.stem: A poet writes, "The moon is a silver coin." What did the poet use?
questions.why: It compares the moon to a coin without like or as.

questions.stem: Which word is the strongest choice for a poem about a storm?
questions.why: Roared is vivid and shows power.

questions.stem: Which line repeats a sound at the beginning of words (alliteration)?
What should a poet do first when writing a poem?
options: write the title last and never change anything
choose a topic and think of images and feelings about it

questions.stem: Which line uses a simile?
options: The kitten was as soft as a cloud.
questions.why: A simile compares with like or as.

questions.stem: A poet revises "The tree was nice" to make it stronger. Which revision is best?
options: The tree was really, really nice.
The old oak stretched its arms toward the sky.
questions.why: It adds a vivid image and personification.

questions.stem: Why might a poet break a line in the middle of a sentence?
options: because poems must have short lines
to create a pause or put weight on a word
questions.why: Line breaks control rhythm and emphasis.

questions.stem: Which poem form has three lines with 5, 7 and 5 syllables?
A poet wants readers to feel calm. Which line fits best?
options: Soft light rests on the quiet lake.
questions.why: Gentle words create a calm mood.

questions.stem: Which revision adds personification? "The wind blew through the town."
options: Blew the wind through the town.
The wind was in the town.
The wind blew hard through the town.
The wind whispered secrets through the town.
questions.why: Whispering secrets gives the wind human actions.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of repeating a line at the end of each stanza?
options: to create a refrain that ties the poem together
questions.why: A refrain makes the poem musical and unified.

questions.stem: Which line shows, rather than tells, that someone is nervous?
options: Her hands trembled as she reached for the door.

questions.stem: A free verse poem is a poem that—
options: does not follow a set rhyme or rhythm pattern
questions.why: Free verse has no fixed pattern.

questions.stem: A poet ends a poem about a grandfather's garden with "Each seed he planted still remembers his hands." What is the effect of this ending?
options: It suggests his love and influence live on after him.
It explains how to plant seeds.
questions.why: The personified seeds show his lasting impact.

questions.stem: Which revision best tightens this line? "The very small little bird sang a very happy song."
options: The very little bird sang happily a song.
The wren sang its bright song.
The small little tiny bird sang.
The bird which was small sang a song that was happy.
questions.why: Precise nouns and fewer words make poetry stronger.

questions.stem: A poet uses short, choppy lines in a poem about a race. Why?
options: The poet ran out of ideas.
The quick rhythm matches the speed and excitement of the race.
Short lines are easier to rhyme.

questions.stem: Which line uses an extended metaphor across two lines?
options: I am worried. / I am tired.
My worry is a heavy coat; / I carry it from room to room.
The sky is blue. / The grass is green.
questions.why: The coat comparison continues in the second line.

questions.stem: A poet changes "I was sad when my friend moved" to "The swing beside mine sways empty now." Why is the revision stronger?
options: It uses a concrete image to show the feeling.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the tone of these lines? "Gray streets, gray sky, / gray thoughts that will not fly."
questions.why: Repeated gray creates a gloomy tone.

questions.stem: In a sonnet, what often happens at the turn (volta)?
options: the poem shifts its idea or answers a problem
questions.why: The volta marks a shift in thought.

questions.stem: A poet wants the last word of a poem to surprise readers. Which technique helps most?
options: building expectations, then breaking the pattern at the end

questions.stem: Which source would give the most reliable facts about sharks?
options: a book by a marine scientist

questions.stem: What is a keyword search?
options: typing important words to find information
questions.why: Keywords help search engines find topics.

questions.stem: When you take notes for a report, you should—
options: write the main facts in your own words
questions.why: Notes in your own words avoid copying.

questions.stem: Why should you write down where you found a fact?
options: so you can give credit and find it again
questions.why: Recording sources is honest and useful.

questions.stem: Which question is best to research for a short report on butterflies?
questions.why: It can be answered with facts.

questions.stem: Which website is probably most reliable for weather facts?
What is a bibliography?
options: a story about a person's life
a list of the sources used in a report

questions.stem: Which is a primary source?
options: a diary written by a soldier during a war
questions.why: Primary sources come from people who were there.

questions.stem: A student finds two websites with different numbers for a mountain's height. What should the student do?
options: check a third reliable source to confirm
questions.why: Confirming with more sources finds the accurate fact.

questions.stem: Which is the best paraphrase of "Honeybees communicate the location of flowers through a dance"?
options: Bees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
Honeybees communicate the location of flowers through a dance.
questions.why: A paraphrase keeps the meaning in new words.

questions.stem: Why is copying a writer's sentences without credit a problem?
options: It is plagiarism—using someone's work as your own.
It makes the report too short.

questions.stem: Which detail suggests a website may NOT be reliable?
options: It has no author and many spelling errors.
questions.why: No author and errors are warning signs.

questions.stem: A student researching volcanoes finds a fact about earthquakes. What should the student ask?
options: Does this fact help answer my research question?

questions.stem: Which is a secondary source about the first moon landing?
options: a magazine article written years later
a recording of the astronauts' voices
a photo taken on the moon

questions.stem: What is the best way to organize notes from several sources?
options: keep them in the order you found them
throw away the ones you don't like
put them all in one sentence
questions.why: Grouping by subtopic helps write sections.

questions.stem: A student quotes an expert. What must the student include?
options: the student's opinion inside the quote
quotation marks and the expert's name

questions.stem: A student's source is a website run by a company that sells the product it reviews. What should the student consider?
options: The site may be biased because it profits from sales.
Bias does not matter in research.
The site is always more accurate.
questions.why: A financial interest can create bias.

questions.stem: Which research question is too narrow for a five-page report?
options: Why are libraries important to communities?
How did public libraries change in the 1900s?
What year was the town's first library card printed?
How do libraries help students learn?
questions.why: A single date cannot fill a report.

questions.stem: A student finds an article from 1995 about cell phones. Why might it be a weak source for current facts?
options: Old articles are always wrong about everything.

questions.stem: Which citation is most complete?
options: Lopez, Ana. "Desert Plants." Science Today, 2024, p. 12.
questions.why: It gives author, title, publication, year and page.

questions.stem: Two sources disagree about why a city grew. How should a strong report handle this?
options: explain both views and which has stronger evidence
choose the source with more pictures

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of synthesizing sources?
options: combining information from several sources to form new understanding

questions.stem: Which search would find the most focused results about coral bleaching in Australia?
options: fish and coral and water and sea
questions.why: Specific keywords and quotation marks focus results.

questions.stem: What should the beginning of a story do?
Which word helps show the order of events in a story?
Which sentence uses dialogue?
What is the problem in a story also called?
Which detail best describes a setting?
options: The dusty road wound past empty fields.
questions.why: It tells where the story happens.

questions.stem: Which ending gives the story a sense of closure?
options: At last, the lost puppy was home, curled up by the fire.
The story is about a puppy.

questions.stem: What does a narrator do?
Which sentence shows a character's feeling through action?
options: Omar stomped up the stairs and slammed his door.

questions.stem: Which revision makes this sentence more vivid? "The dog ran."
options: The scruffy dog bolted across the muddy yard.

questions.stem: A writer wants to slow down an exciting moment. What should the writer do?
options: add sensory details and the character's thoughts

questions.stem: Which transition shows a jump in time?
Which is first-person point of view?
options: She grabbed her bag and ran.
I grabbed my bag and ran.

questions.stem: What makes a narrative's conflict interesting?
options: the character wants something and faces obstacles

questions.stem: Which line of dialogue best reveals a character's personality?
options: "Rules? I make my own rules," Zain smirked.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best hook for a story?
options: I will tell you about a river.
The day the river turned purple, nobody in Elm Town could explain it.

questions.stem: Why might a writer begin a story in the middle of the action?
options: to grab the reader immediately and build suspense

questions.stem: Which revision uses pacing to build suspense?
options: The door opened and someone walked in slowly and sat down.
There was a door in the house.
questions.why: Short fragments slow the moment and build tension.

questions.stem: A writer includes a flashback. What must the writer make clear?
options: when the story moves to the past and back

questions.stem: Which ending best shows how the main character has changed?
options: This time, Maya raised her hand first—no shaking voice, no second thoughts.
questions.why: It contrasts with her earlier fear.

questions.stem: What is the effect of writing a narrative in present tense?
options: It makes events feel immediate, as if happening now.
It makes the story about the future.
It turns the story into a poem.

questions.stem: Which detail is LEAST useful in a story about a girl's first swim race?
options: her heart pounding on the starting block
the price of bread at the bakery
the cold splash of the water
questions.why: It does not develop the story.

questions.stem: A writer reveals a character's thoughts through an unreliable narrator. What does this create?
options: doubt about what is really true, making readers think
questions.why: Unreliable narrators create tension and questions.

questions.stem: Which sentence states an opinion?
options: There are 30 students in my class.

questions.stem: Which reason best supports "Students should read every day"?
Which word introduces a reason?
What should the conclusion of an opinion piece do?
options: ask the reader to stop reading

questions.stem: Which is a fact, not an opinion?
Which opinion sentence is clearest?
options: Our class should plant a school garden.

questions.stem: Which detail supports "Pets make good companions"?
options: Pets can help people feel less lonely.
Pet stores are open on Monday.
questions.why: It explains why pets are good companions.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence is strongest for "Schools should serve healthy lunches"?
options: A study found students who eat healthy lunches focus better in class.

questions.stem: What is a counterclaim?
options: an opposing argument the writer answers

questions.stem: Which transition best introduces a counterclaim?
Which sentence best responds to the counterclaim "Homework takes away free time"?
options: I don't care about free time.
However, short daily homework builds habits that save time later.
questions.why: It answers the counterclaim with a reason.

questions.stem: Which claim is most arguable (people could disagree)?
options: Video games can help students learn.
Video games were invented in the 1900s.

questions.stem: Why should a writer explain how evidence supports a claim?
Which tone is best for a persuasive letter to the principal?
Which sentence is a precise, arguable claim?
options: Our school should replace one weekly test with a project to deepen learning.

questions.stem: A writer uses the statement "Everyone knows phones are harmful." What is weak about it?
options: It is a sweeping generalization without evidence.

questions.stem: Which evidence is most credible for an argument about air pollution?
options: data from an environmental protection agency
a comment on a social media post

questions.stem: What does it mean to rebut a counterclaim?
options: to explain why the opposing argument is weaker
questions.why: A rebuttal answers the other side.

questions.stem: Which revision avoids an emotional appeal and uses logic instead?
options: Imagine the tears of families who lost loved ones!
Only cruel people oppose bike lanes.
Bike lanes reduced accidents by 30% in nearby cities.

questions.stem: A writer's conclusion includes a call to action. What does that mean?
options: it asks readers to do something specific
questions.why: A call to action urges response.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to organize an argument essay?
options: claim, reasons with evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal, conclusion

questions.stem: What is the purpose of informative writing?
options: to teach or explain facts about a topic

questions.stem: Which sentence is a good topic sentence for a paragraph about frogs?
options: Frogs have amazing ways to survive.

questions.stem: Which detail belongs in a paragraph about how plants grow?
Which text feature helps readers find sections?
Which word introduces an example?
Which sentence defines a term?
options: A habitat is the place where an animal lives.
questions.why: It explains what the word means.

questions.stem: What should an informative conclusion do?
Which sentence uses a precise, domain-specific word?
options: The volcano let out hot stuff.
The volcano was big and bad.

questions.stem: A writer explains how to make a kite. Which structure fits best?
Which transition shows a contrast between two facts?
Which detail best supports the idea that camels survive in deserts?
options: Camels can go many days without drinking water.

questions.stem: Why might a writer add a diagram to an explanation of the water cycle?
Which sentence keeps a formal style?
options: Scientists study the effects of pollution on rivers.
Scientists totally check out rivers and stuff.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to group facts in an essay about the planets?
options: by planet, with one paragraph each
in the order you found them

questions.stem: Which thesis is strongest for an essay about recycling?
options: Recycling conserves resources, saves energy and reduces landfill waste.
Recycling is a thing people do.

questions.stem: A writer explains the causes of a famine. Which organization fits?
Which sentence best integrates a quotation?
options: "Bees pollinate a third of our crops." Bees.
According to biologist Dr. Reem Said, "Bees pollinate a third of our crops."

questions.stem: Which revision removes unnecessary information from an essay on solar energy?
options: Delete the statistic on energy savings.
Delete the definition of solar panels.
Delete the sentence about the writer's favorite movie.

questions.stem: Why should a writer anticipate the reader's questions?
options: to answer them and make the explanation complete

questions.stem: Which sentence best concludes an essay on ocean plastic?
options: Reducing single-use plastic today can protect ocean life for generations.

questions.stem: Which detail is most precise?
options: About 8 million tons of plastic enter the oceans each year.
A lot of plastic goes in the ocean.

questions.stem: In "The baseball player swung the bat," what does bat mean?
options: a wooden stick used in sports
questions.why: A player swings a wooden bat.

questions.stem: In "We saw a bat flying at night," what does bat mean?
options: a stick for hitting a ball
questions.why: Flying at night tells us it is an animal.

questions.stem: In "Please wave goodbye," what does wave mean?
options: move your hand back and forth
questions.why: You wave your hand to say goodbye.

questions.stem: In "The ring on her finger sparkled," what does ring mean?
In "The bark of the tree was rough," what does bark mean?
options: the outside covering of a tree

questions.stem: In "Turn on the light," what does light mean?
In "The box was light enough to carry," what does light mean?
questions.why: Easy to carry means not heavy.

questions.stem: In "The coach will train the team," what does train mean?
options: the long part of a dress

questions.stem: In "She will file the papers," what does file mean?
Which sentence uses fair to mean "a festival with rides and games"?
options: The rules were fair to everyone.
We rode the Ferris wheel at the fair.
questions.why: Rides and games happen at a fair.

questions.stem: In "The pitcher threw a fast ball," which other meaning of pitcher does NOT fit?
options: the player who throws the ball
questions.why: Here pitcher is a player, not a jug.

questions.stem: In "Don't bear the weight alone," what does bear mean?
questions.why: Bear the weight means carry it.

questions.stem: In "Mom made a match between the two socks," what does match mean?
options: a small stick that makes fire

questions.stem: In "The scientist will present her findings," what does present mean?
options: show or explain to an audience

questions.stem: Which sentence uses object as a verb meaning "to disagree"?
options: The object of the game is to win.
I object to that unfair rule.
The object on the table is a cup.
questions.why: Object as a verb means oppose.

questions.stem: In "The general feeling was hopeful," what does general mean?
questions.why: General feeling means most people's feeling.

questions.stem: Which clue word helps you know the meaning of seal in "The seal balanced a ball on its nose"?
options: balanced a ball on its nose
questions.why: That action points to the animal.

questions.stem: In "The novel had a strong plot," which meaning of novel fits?
options: a long book that tells a story

questions.stem: In "The idea was novel, so no one had tried it," what does novel mean?
questions.why: No one had tried it, so it was new.

questions.stem: What is foreshadowing?
options: a hint about something that will happen later
questions.why: Foreshadowing gives clues about later events.

questions.stem: Dark clouds gather as the hikers start up the mountain. What might this foreshadow?
questions.why: Dark clouds hint at a storm.

questions.stem: A character says, "I have a bad feeling about this." What does this do?
options: hints that something will go wrong

questions.stem: In a story, a boy notices a loose board on a bridge. Later, he trips there. The loose board was—
questions.why: It hinted at the later event.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an example of foreshadowing?
options: Lina didn't notice the cracked ice near the shore.
questions.why: The cracked ice hints at danger.

questions.stem: Why do authors use foreshadowing?
options: to build suspense and prepare readers

questions.stem: A dog growls at a new visitor at the start of a story. What could this hint?
options: the visitor may not be trustworthy
questions.why: The dog's reaction hints at the visitor.

questions.stem: At the start of a story, Grandpa gives Mia an old compass "just in case." Later she gets lost. How does the compass work in the plot?
options: It foreshadows that she will need it.
questions.why: The gift hints she will need it.

questions.stem: Which detail most likely foreshadows a surprise ending?
options: The neighbor had a red car.
The quiet neighbor always kept his garage door locked.
questions.why: A locked secret hints at a reveal.

questions.stem: How is foreshadowing different from a flashback?
options: Foreshadowing hints at the future; a flashback shows the past.
A flashback hints at the future.
questions.why: They point in opposite directions in time.

questions.stem: A chapter ends: "If only she had read the last line of the letter." What does this create?
options: suspense about what the letter said
questions.why: Readers want to know what happens.

questions.stem: Which is the best evidence that an event was foreshadowed?
options: An earlier detail hinted that it would happen.
questions.why: Foreshadowing is shown by earlier hints.

questions.stem: Mysterious music plays when a character opens a door in a film. This is like foreshadowing because—
options: it signals that something important or scary will happen

questions.stem: An author mentions a broken lock three times early in a mystery. What is the most likely purpose?
options: to plant a clue that will matter in the solution

questions.stem: How can foreshadowing make an ending feel satisfying rather than random?
options: Earlier hints make the ending feel earned and believable.
questions.why: Hints prepare readers for the outcome.

questions.stem: A story's first line is "Nobody in the village believed the old warning about the river." What does it foreshadow?
options: that the warning will come true

questions.stem: Which is an example of a 'red herring' rather than true foreshadowing?
options: a clue that misleads readers toward the wrong suspect
a hint that correctly predicts the ending

questions.stem: In a tragedy, the hero says, "Nothing can stop me now." What does this line likely foreshadow?
questions.why: Overconfidence often hints at a fall.

questions.stem: Why might an author foreshadow subtly instead of obviously?
options: to surprise readers while keeping the ending believable
questions.why: Subtle hints balance surprise and logic.

questions.stem: What is a pun?
options: a joke that plays on words with two meanings or similar sounds
a kind of poem with 14 lines

questions.stem: Why is this a pun? "The math book looked sad because it had too many problems."
options: Problems means math questions and also troubles.
questions.why: The word problems has two meanings.

questions.stem: "I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough." What two meanings does dough have?
Which sentence is a pun?
options: The bicycle fell over because it was two-tired.

questions.stem: "Why did the cookie go to the doctor? It felt crummy." What makes it funny?
options: Crummy means full of crumbs and also feeling bad.

questions.stem: Which word is used for wordplay in "Time flies like an arrow"?
questions.why: Flies can mean moves fast or insects.

questions.stem: A pun usually makes readers—
options: laugh or groan at a clever double meaning

questions.stem: "The scarecrow won an award because he was outstanding in his field." Explain the pun.
options: Outstanding in his field means excellent and standing in a field.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a homophone pun?
options: The knight was afraid of the dark night.

questions.stem: What makes this wordplay? "A boiled egg in the morning is hard to beat."
options: Hard to beat means excellent, and eggs are beaten.

questions.stem: Why do writers use puns in titles of articles?
options: to catch readers' attention with humor

questions.stem: "I'm reading a book about anti-gravity. It's impossible to put down." What is the pun?
options: Impossible to put down means very interesting and won't fall.

questions.stem: Which is NOT an example of wordplay?
options: The river flows to the sea.
I'm on a seafood diet: I see food and eat it.
Bakers knead the dough they need.
Seven days without a pun makes one weak.

questions.stem: "Seven days without a pun makes one weak." What two meanings are combined?
options: one week and one weak person

questions.stem: In a play, a dying character says, "Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a grave man." What is the effect of the pun?
options: It mixes humor with the seriousness of death (grave = serious / tomb).
questions.why: Grave has two meanings, adding dark humor.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a pun to make a serious point?
options: Some politicians promise to raise standards, but only their own salaries rise.
questions.why: Raise is used with two meanings for irony.

questions.stem: A store called "Curl Up & Dye" is a hair salon. What makes the name clever?
options: Dye sounds like die, and curl up has two meanings.
questions.why: It plays on sound and meaning.

questions.stem: Why might puns be hard to translate into another language?
options: The double meaning depends on words in one language.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a spoonerism (swapping sounds for wordplay)?
options: "You hissed my mystery lecture" for "You missed my history lecture."

questions.stem: A speaker says, "We need a crosswalk near school because many cars drive fast there." What is the reason?
Which is evidence a speaker could use to support "Our library needs more books"?
options: Half the shelves are empty, and students wait weeks for popular books.

questions.stem: What should a good listener do to find a speaker's main point?
options: listen for what the speaker wants the audience to think or do
questions.why: The main point is the speaker's message.

questions.stem: A speaker says, "I think we should have a class pet. Pets teach responsibility." What is the claim?
options: We should have a class pet.
questions.why: The claim is the speaker's position.

questions.stem: Which question helps you check a speaker's evidence?
options: What color is the speaker's shirt?
How does the speaker know this?
questions.why: Asking how they know checks evidence.

questions.stem: A speaker gives a reason but no facts. What is missing?
A speaker says, "Recycling helps. Last year our school recycled 2 tons of paper." What kind of evidence is this?
Which reason is NOT relevant to "The school day should start later"?
questions.why: Tables do not relate to start times.

questions.stem: A speaker quotes a doctor about sleep. Why does this strengthen the speech?
How can you tell whether a speaker's claim is supported?
options: See if the speaker is loud.
Check whether facts, examples or expert views back it up.
Check if the speech is long.

questions.stem: A speaker says, "Everyone agrees with me." What is the problem?
options: It is not evidence and may not be true.

questions.stem: A speaker argues for a new park and says, "Studies show green spaces lower stress, and our town has none within two miles." Evaluate this support.
options: It combines research with a local fact, so it is strong.
questions.why: Research plus local data is strong support.

questions.stem: Which question best evaluates a speaker's statistic?
options: Is the number odd or even?
Where did the number come from, and is it recent?

questions.stem: A speaker uses a dramatic story about one student to argue a rule affects everyone. What is the weakness?
options: One example may not represent everyone.

questions.stem: Which response best summarizes how a speaker supported a claim?
options: She argued for longer recess using research on focus and teachers' observations.
questions.why: It names the claim and the evidence.

questions.stem: A speaker ignores a strong opposing argument. How does this affect the speech?
options: It weakens credibility because listeners may doubt the claim.

questions.stem: In science, what does observe mean?
In a math or science text, what is a measurement?
options: the size or amount of something found with a tool

questions.stem: In social studies, a community is—
options: a group of people living in the same area

questions.stem: What does habitat mean in a science text?
options: the natural home of a plant or animal
questions.why: A habitat is a home in nature.

questions.stem: In "The liquid will evaporate in the sun," what does evaporate mean?
options: change into a gas and disappear into the air

questions.stem: In history, what is a timeline?
options: a line showing events in order of time

questions.stem: In "The colonists traded furs for tools," what does traded mean?
A science text says a material is a conductor. What does it do?
options: allows heat or electricity to pass through

questions.stem: In "The region has a dry climate," what does climate mean?
options: the usual weather of a place over a long time

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "Plants use sunlight to make food in a process called ____."
In "The government passed a new law," what does government mean?
options: the group that makes and enforces rules for a country

questions.stem: In "Erosion gradually reshaped the canyon," what does erosion mean?
options: the wearing away of land by water, wind or ice

questions.stem: In "The economy grew as exports increased," what are exports?
options: goods sent to other countries to sell

questions.stem: A science article says the results were "statistically significant." What does it most likely mean?
options: the results are unlikely to be due to chance
questions.why: Significance means not likely by chance.

questions.stem: In "The treaty ended the conflict between the nations," what is a treaty?
Which word best completes the sentence? "The cell's ____ controls its activities."
questions.why: The nucleus is the control center.

questions.stem: Which word means to tell how two things are alike?
What does it mean to explain an answer?
options: tell why or how it is true

questions.stem: Which word means to put things in order from first to last?
A test asks you to identify the main idea. What should you do?
options: find and name the main idea

questions.stem: What does summarize mean?
options: tell the most important parts briefly

questions.stem: Which word means a guess based on clues?
A question asks you to justify your answer. What should you add?
options: reasons or evidence that support it

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The author uses facts to ____ her claim."
What does it mean to analyze a poem?
options: examine its parts closely to understand it

questions.stem: Which word means the effect something has?
In "The data reveal a pattern," what does reveal mean?
A prompt asks you to evaluate an argument. What should you do?
options: judge how strong and convincing it is, with reasons

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The two studies reached ____ conclusions, so scientists debated them."
In "The evidence is insufficient to prove the claim," what does insufficient mean?
What does it mean to synthesize information?
options: combine ideas from several sources into one understanding

questions.stem: Which word best describes a claim based on careful reasoning?

questions.stem: Which sentence is active voice?
options: The ball was kicked by Maya.
questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage

questions.stem: In "The cake was eaten by the kids," who did the action?
questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
